name: Hawaii

notes: Food is subject to the general excise tax like any other sale, with the county's 0.5% surcharge. Lower-income residents can claim the refundable Food/Excise Tax Credit instead: $220 a person with income under $15,000, falling to $70 a person at $50,000 to $60,000 (single filers qualify below $40,000, others below $60,000); it isn't taken out here.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and spirits pay the general excise tax plus the state liquor tax, left out here: $5.98 a gallon on spirits, $1.38 on still wine, $2.12 on sparkling wine, $0.85 on coolers, $0.93 on beer and $0.54 on draft beer (containers of 5 gallons or more since January 1, 2026, Act 90 of 2025).

Cigarettes and other tobacco pay the general excise tax plus the cigarette and tobacco tax, left out here: 18 cents a cigarette ($3.60 a pack) since January 1, 2026 (Act 95 of 2025; 16 cents before), 70% of the wholesale price on other tobacco products and on e-cigarettes and e-liquids (since January 1, 2024), and 50% on large cigars.
Household supplies: diapers are taxed like other goods; Hawaii has no exemption for them.
Personal care products: menstrual products are taxed like other goods; a 2026 bill to exempt them (SB 2935) was not enacted.
Barber and beauty services: the general excise tax applies to services, haircuts and salons included.
Clothing is taxed; Hawaii has no sales tax holiday.
Laundry and dry cleaning: the general excise tax applies to laundry and dry cleaning, as to other services.

Gasoline pays the general excise tax and the county surcharge on its price before fuel taxes (as the Federal Highway Administration reports it), plus per-gallon fuel taxes left out here: 16 cents state and 16.5 cents (Honolulu), 24 cents (Maui County), 23 cents (Hawaii County) or 17 cents (Kauai) county, and the $1.05-a-barrel environmental response tax (2.5 cents a gallon).
Auto repair labor: the general excise tax applies to repair labor, as to other services.

The general excise tax is levied on the business, not the buyer. Sellers may pass it on at up to 4.712% of the price before tax (4.166% in Kalawao County, which has no surcharge), which is the same 4.5% of what the buyer pays; the 4.5% is used here. The county surcharges run through December 31, 2030; the counties have said they will ask the 2027 Legislature to extend them (reported).

Hotel and vacation-rental stays pay the general excise tax plus the state transient accommodations tax, 11% since January 1, 2026 (Act 96 of 2025, the "green fee", through 2030; 10.25% before), and a 3% county transient accommodations tax in every county (Honolulu since December 14, 2021, Maui since November 1, 2021, Kauai since late 2021 and Hawaii County since January 1, 2022); none is counted here. The tax on cruise fares in Act 96 is blocked by a federal court order (DOTAX Announcement 2026-01).
gaps: Hawaii levies a general excise tax on sellers rather than a sales tax: 4% state plus a 0.5% county surcharge in every county except Kalawao. It applies to nearly all sales, including groceries and services. Sellers may pass it on at up to 4.712% of the price before tax (4.166% in Kalawao County), which is 4.5% of what the buyer pays; 4.5% is used here. The county surcharges run through December 31, 2030.

programs: Enterprise Zones are mapped from the state's layer (18 zones, April 2026); Act 182 of 2026 lengthens the benefits for businesses joining from July 1, 2026 (up to nine years, twelve for manufacturing and agriculture). The Department of Business, Economic Development and Tourism's page says 20 zones exist but lists 18, and names a West Maui zone where the layer has Napili. Also mapped: the Hawaii Community Development Authority's six districts and Honolulu's adopted TOD special districts. Hawaii has no tax increment districts; on November 3, 2026 voters decide Question 2, which would let counties issue bonds repaid from property-tax growth in designated districts (reported). No Main Street program map was found.

warn.text: Urban Honolulu draws many visitors (Waikiki and Pearl Harbor), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the area as a whole: its seasonal homes (3.8%) and its 250 lodging places (0.7 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, since a resort's few very large hotels count as only a handful of lodging places (the state's visitor plant inventory places about 40,900 visitor units in its tracts), though 16 of its 132 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Not mapped: Honolulu's four special improvement districts: the Waikiki business improvement district (No. 1, Ordinance 00-40, amended by 01-22), the Downtown Honolulu business improvement district (No. 2, Bill 51, Ordinance 25-47, signed October 20, 2025, which expanded and renamed the Fort Street Mall district: roughly Nuuanu Avenue to Richards Street and Nimitz Highway to Beretania Street, funded by assessments on non-residential property, for five years as reported by Spectrum News), and the Waikiki Beach (No. 3, Ordinance 15-11) and Waikiki transportation management (No. 4, Ordinance 17-58) districts (Office of the Mayor; Revised Ordinances of Honolulu, chapter 28).

programs: Not mapped: the Kailua Village Business Improvement District in Historic Kailua Village along Aliʻi Drive, established by Hawaii County Ordinance 07-171, effective December 11, 2007 (County Code chapter 35 annex, which lists no ordinance ending it); no map of its boundary was found.

warn: The wildfire of August 8, 2023 damaged or destroyed about 2,200 buildings in and around Lahaina (FEMA estimate, as reported by Maui Now, August 12, 2023). This page's household, store and job figures mostly come from before the fire, and the business listings still show the shops along Front Street, while the state's December 2025 visitor plant inventory lists no visitor units in two of Lahaina's three census tracts; the readings here describe Lahaina as it was, not as it is now.
